title: Five questions before I name a ship
subtitle: The brief matters more than the brochure. Most of a good voyage is decided before a ship is chosen.

text: The first thing I need isn't a destination. It's a temperament.
sub: Two travellers can want the same coastline and need entirely different ships. Naming the ship first is how people end up on the wrong one.

title: Five questions before I name a ship

items.head: What did you last regret?
items.body: The clearest signal in the whole conversation. Regret is far more specific than preference.

items.head: How many ports is too many?
items.body: Some want seven. Some want three and a long lunch. No correct answer, only yours.

items.head: Dinner at eight, or whenever?
items.body: Fixed seating, open dining and a small ship's single restaurant are three different holidays.

items.head: Who else is coming?
items.body: A cabin for two is a different problem to a family across three cabins on separate decks.

items.head: What would feel oversold?
items.body: Everyone has a line. Yours tells me which ships to leave off the list entirely.

text: Half of any recommendation is removal.
sub: The short list is short because things were taken out of it. What you never see is most of the work, and most of the reason it is worth having.

quote: Most of what I do isn't booking travel - it's editing it.

points.label: The line
points.value: Service style, temperament, and how much ceremony you can comfortably stand.

points.label: The ship
points.value: Size, motion, and whether it can berth where the large ships must anchor.

points.label: The season
points.value: Shoulder dates buy quieter ports more reliably than any upgrade ever will.

points.label: The cabin
points.value: Chosen last, on the deck plan, once the first three are properly settled.

title: Answer the first one in the comments
body: What did you last regret on a voyage - the ship, the season, the itinerary, or the cabin? I read every reply and I'll tell you what I'd change.
